bib.title: Keep CALM and Explore: Language Models for Action Generation in Text-based Games

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Keep CALM and Explore: Language Models for Action Generation in Text-based Games", Shunyu Yao, Rohan Rao, Matthew Hausknecht, Karthik Narasimhan (Princeton, Microsoft Research). EMNLP 2020, pages 8736–8754 (arXiv 2010.02903).

COVERAGE: Read all 86,671 of 86,671 chars, including Appendices A–D, Tables 4–5 and Figures 9–16. I only skimmed the references. Figures 10, 15 and 16 are letter-spaced trajectory dumps. I read them and found nothing evaluative beyond what the captions say. File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/08-eval/sources/yao-2020-keep-calm-explore.pdf

CLAIMS
- claim: The headline result is a 69% relative improvement in average normalised score over the previous handicap-free best (NAIL). In absolute terms that is 9.4% against 5.6% normalised score. The language model never saw transcripts of the evaluation games.
  number: 69% relative; 9.4% vs 5.6%
  setup: 28 Jericho games. CALM (GPT-2, 117M) proposes top-30 actions and a DRRN picks among them. Average of 5 seeds.
  quote: "CALM (GPT-2) outperforms CALM (n-gram) and NAIL by 4.4% and 3.8% on absolute normalized scores, respectively. Relatively, this represents almost a 69% improvement over NAIL."
  where: p.8 (§5.2); Table 2 "avg. norm 9.4% 5.5% 5.6% 10.8% 13.0%"
- claim: Normalised score is raw score divided by the game's maximum score, and the paper reports only its average across games, because score scales differ between games.
  number: none
  setup: Jericho, all 28 games
  quote: "To take into account different score scales across games, we consider both the raw score and the normalized score (raw score divided by maximum score), and only report the average normalized score across games."
  where: p.8 (§5.2)
- claim: The generalisation holdout is that the language model is trained only on transcripts that do not overlap with the 28 evaluation games.
  number: 28 games
  setup: ClubFloyd human transcripts (426 transcripts, 590 games, 223,527 context-action pairs)
  quote: "Importantly, both models are trained only on transcripts that do not overlap with the 28 Jericho games we evaluate on."
  where: p.6 (§4.2)
- claim: When the authors relax the holdout and add 8 transcripts of the evaluation games, the score rises from 9.4% to 10.9%, which beats the handicap-assisted KG-A2C (10.8%). The gains, however, did not come mainly on the games whose transcripts were added.
  number: 10.9% vs 9.4%; 8 scripts
  setup: CALM (w/ Jericho) variant, 5 seeds
  quote: "Counter-intuitively, we find that the greatest performance gains aren't on games featured in the heldout transcripts."; Table 3 "CALM (w/ Jericho) 10.9%"; App. D: "CALM (w/ Jericho) is significantly better than CALM (GPT-2) on the games of Temple and Deephome ... which are not the games with ClubFloyd scripts added. On the other hand, games like 905 and moonlit have scripts added, but do not get improved."
  where: p.9 (§5.3); p.13 (App. D)
- claim: Each game's score comes from five seeds. The final score of a run is the mean of its last 100 training episodes. The ablations were run once each.
  number: 5 seeds; 100 episodes; 1 trial for ablations
  setup: DRRN trained on 8 parallel environments for 10^6 steps
  quote: "The final score of a training run is taken to be the average score of the final 100 episodes during training. For each game, we train five independent agents with different random seeds and report the average score. For model variants in § 5.3 we only run one trail."
  where: p.7 (§4.3)
- claim: Variance across seeds is large on some games. On library the standard deviation is about half the mean.
  number: library 9.02 (±5.07); zork1 30.39 (±3.01); inhumane 25.73 (±2.93)
  setup: Table 5, std over 5 trials, only for CALM GPT-2, n-gram and w/ Jericho
  quote: "library 9.02 (± 5.07)"; "Note that some scores are only based on one trial. CALM (GPT-2), CALM (ngram) and CALM (w/ Jericho) are based on five trails and the standard deviation is given."
  where: p.14 (Table 5)
- claim: Validation loss and accuracy on held-out human data are not good enough to evaluate an action generator. A state can have many valid actions, and the human actions in the data may be suboptimal or invalid. The authors therefore score candidates against Jericho walkthroughs.
  number: none
  setup: ClubFloyd validation set compared with Jericho optimal walkthroughs
  quote: "Metrics like validation loss or accuracy on validation set of our ClubFloyd data are not sufficient to evaluate CALM ... This is because: 1) there can be multiple admissible actions in each state, and 2) the human actions in the trajectories are not guaranteed to be optimal or even admissible."
  where: p.7 (§5.1)
- claim: The standalone evaluation measures precision and recall of admissible actions and recall of the gold action at top-k. At k=15 the candidates cover about 30% of admissible actions. Raising k increases recall but lowers precision, which is the exploration versus exploitation trade-off.
  number: ~30% at k=15; GPT-2 +10% admissible recall from k=15 to 30; +20% gold recall vs n-gram at k=30
  setup: walkthroughs of 28 games, metrics averaged per game
  quote: "the top k = 15 actions of CALM (GPT-2 and n-gram) are both expected to contain around 30% of all admissible actions in each walkthrough state. However, when k goes from 15 to 30, CALM (GPT-2) can come up with 10% more admissible actions"; "the top-30 actions from CALM (GPT-2) contain the gold action in 20% more game states than CALM (n-gram)."
  where: p.7 (§5.1), Fig. 4
- claim: Without the admissible-action handicap, CALM beats both handicapped baselines on 8 of 28 games. The authors offer two guesses why: CALM may filter out useless admissible actions, or it may find actions the handicap's state-change detection misses.
  number: 8 of 28; inhumane 25.7 vs KG-A2C 3
  setup: Table 2
  quote: "On 8 out of 28 games (underlined in Table 2), CALM (GPT-2) outperforms both DRRN and KG-A2C despite the latter having access to ground-truth admissible actions."; "it is possible that CALM sometimes discover admissible actions even the handicap cannot (due to the imperfection of state change detection)."
  where: p.8 (§5.2)
- claim: The handicap is an oracle that queries simulator internals. It costs about as much as a GPT-2 pass and may not exist outside Jericho.
  number: none
  setup: Jericho framework
  quote: "testing each action's admissibility by accessing the underlying simulator states and load-and-save functions. As a result, the handicap runs no faster than a GPT-2 inference pass, and could in fact be unavailable for games outside Jericho."
  where: p.6 (§4.1)
- claim: The final-score metric understates what the agent found. If the RL agent had learned from the best trajectories it saw while exploring, the score would have been 14.7%, higher than every model in the paper.
  number: 14.7%
  setup: Fig. 6, CALM (GPT-2)
  quote: "If RL can fully exploit and learn from the trajectories experienced under the CALM action space for each game, the average normalized score would be 14.7%, higher than any model in Table 2, both with and without handicaps."
  where: p.8–9 (§5.3)
- claim: Ablations show the language model alone is weak. A random policy over CALM's candidates scores 1.8%, a GPT-2 without pre-training scores 6.8%, and k=10 scores 5.6%. An off-the-shelf GPT-2 does not produce parseable actions.
  number: 1.8%; 6.8%; 5.6% (k=10); k=20/40 at 9.6%/9.2%
  setup: Table 3, one trial each
  quote: "CALM (random agent) performs a poor score of 1.8%"; "CALM (w/o PT) 6.8%"; "CALM (k = 10) 5.6%"
  where: p.8–9 (Table 3, §5.3)
- claim: Scores at k=20, 30 and 40 are similar on average but differ game by game, so an average can hide per-game differences.
  number: none
  setup: Table 3/5
  quote: "though k = 20, 30, 40 achieve similar overall performance, they achieve different results for different games."
  where: p.9
- claim: Text games remain far from solved. Even the handicapped DRRN reaches only 13.0% normalised.
  number: 13.0%
  setup: Table 2
  quote: "From the results in Table 2, it is safe to conclude that text-based games are still far from being solved."
  where: p.9 (§6)

LIMITS:
- The ablations use one seed each, and standard deviations are given only for three models. The paper runs no significance tests, so the 8-of-28 count and the gaps between ablations are not checked against variance.
- The authors concede that DRRN does not converge to the best scores seen in exploration (Fig. 6). They also say a different k per game might help.
- Two observations of mine, which the paper does not draw:
  - Normalisation divides by the maximum score without subtracting a game's starting score. Advent starts at 36 of 350, so it adds the same ~10% to every method. Many games score 0 for every method.
  - The "unseen games" holdout is at the level of games, not genres or domains.
- The source is dated. It predates LLM agents, and its baselines (NAIL, KG-A2C, DRRN) are from 2019–2020. The "69%" is relative to a 5.6% baseline.

BUILDS ON: Jericho benchmark (Hausknecht et al., 2019a), DRRN (He et al., 2015), NAIL (Hausknecht et al., 2019b), KG-A2C (Ammanabrolu and Hausknecht, 2020), GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019), separate replay buffer for best trajectories (Narasimhan et al., 2015), FastText admissibility filter (Joulin et al., 2017), TextWorld (Côté et al., 2018), seq2seq action generation (Tao et al., 2018).

CODE: Nothing worth keeping. Code is linked at github.com/princeton-nlp/calm-textgame (p.1 footnote). The evaluation metric definitions (Eq. 7–9, p.7) are short: prec_a(k) = (1/l) Σ |A_t ∩ A_LM(c_t,k)| / k; rec_a(k) = (1/l) Σ |A_t ∩ A_LM| / |A_t|; rec_g(k) = (1/l) Σ |{a_t} ∩ A_LM|.

FIGURES:
- Fig. 4 (p.6): "Precision and recall of gold and admissible actions generated by CALM, evaluated on walkthrough trajectories of 28 games... k is the number of actions." It shows the precision/recall trade-off as k grows in a single picture.
- Fig. 6 (p.8): "Final scores (blue) and maximum scores (normalized) seen during exploration (red) for CALM (GPT-2)." It shows the gap between final and best-seen scores, which is a metric-design point.
- Fig. 5 (p.8): per-game difference against NAIL. It shows the average gain is concentrated in a few games (detective, snacktime, inhumane).

PROBLEMS:
- pypdf printed one FloatObject warning, which is harmless. Text extraction is clean, apart from the letter-spaced appendix figures 10 and 15.
- The text contradicts itself on game count: 590 games in §1/§4.1 but "spanning over 500 games" in App. A. The paper also writes "trail" for "trial".
- The PDF contains no embedded instructions.
